name: buttercream frosting
instructions:
RATIO — 2:1 SUGAR:BUTTER, MILK/CREAM TO DESIRED RUNNINESS. Ratio still pending experiments (see notes).

Beat room-temp butter until pale and fluffy (~3 min). Gradually add powdered sugar at the 2:1 ratio. Add 1 tsp vanilla, pinch of salt, then 2-4 tbsp milk or heavy cream until you hit the texture you want — less for stiff piping, more for spreading.

CRITICAL — ADD FAT SLOWLY / INCREMENTALLY: if the butter is on the softer side (or melted), incorporate it into the powdered sugar slowly rather than dumping it all in. Too much fat overwhelms the sugar and tips the frosting from matte-fluffy into shiny/greasy — one-way trip; can't be walked back without a lot more powdered sugar. Start LESS than the target, whip in, inspect, add more only if needed.
notes:
=== RATIO — 2:1 SUGAR:BUTTER (PENDING EXPERIMENTS) ===

Working ratio: 2 parts powdered sugar to 1 part butter (by volume — e.g., 2 cups powdered sugar : 1 cup butter). Milk or heavy cream added to hit desired runniness. This is what I'm currently using; still need to run experiments to confirm it's the right landing.

=== POWDERED SUGAR, NOT GRANULATED ===

The cornstarch in powdered sugar matters for texture. Granulated sugar doesn't dissolve into the fat the way powdered does; you'd end up with a gritty frosting.

=== BUTTER MUST BE ROOM TEMP ===

Too cold and it won't whip. Too warm and it slumps into a loose mess. Room temp is the target — pale-and-fluffy result depends on it.

=== ADD FAT SLOWLY / INCREMENTALLY — DON'T OVERWHELM THE POWDERED SUGAR ===

Add the butter incrementally, especially if it's on the softer side or if it was melted at any point. The powdered sugar can only absorb so much fat before the frosting tips from matte-and-fluffy into shiny-and-greasy — one-way trip. Practical: start with LESS butter than the ratio calls for, whip it in, inspect, add more only if needed. Easier to correct too-stiff than too-loose.

=== SHELF-STABLE — CAN SIT OUT ===

Buttercream is shelf-stable — a frosted cake can sit at room temperature for hours without needing refrigeration. Same shelf-stability class as bakers-frosting. Contrast with cream-cheese-frosting and strawberry-compote (NOT shelf-stable) and chocolate-ganache (in between — technically not shelf-stable due to the cream, but more stable than cream cheese frosting or compote).

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- cream-cheese-frosting: 2:1 cream cheese:butter, then 1:1 fat:sugar. Tangy and less sweet-forward; softer texture; needs refrigeration.
- bakers-frosting: crisco + water + cream of tartar version — shelf-stable at room temp, holds piping detail, more neutral flavor. Used to live as a variant here; split into its own recipe.
- caramel-frosting: caramelized dairy alternative in the same cake-topping category.
- chocolate-ganache: chocolate + cream, looser format.
